objections.title: A first cause isn’t the God of theism
objections.whoRaises: Typical skeptic; many popular critics of cosmological arguments
objections.objection: Even if the argument gets you to some first cause, it can’t tell you what that cause is like. For all it shows, the cause could be an impersonal force, a quantum field, or a committee of gods. Calling it ‘God’ is a bait-and-switch.
objections.reply:
Feser calls this objection common but entirely ungrounded. The Aristotelian argument doesn’t reach a vague ‘something’; it reaches something **purely actual**, and pure actuality has consequences:

1. No potential means no change: **immutable**.
2. No change means no time: **eternal**.
3. No change or time means no matter: **immaterial, incorporeal**.
4. No unrealized potential means no privation: **perfect** and **fully good**.
5. Nothing to differentiate two such beings: **one**.
6. The source of all actualizing power: **omnipotent**.
7. By proportionate causality, the forms of everything must be in it abstractly: **intelligent** and **omniscient**.

That is the traditional concept of God, and it is derived, not assumed. A fuller defense of each attribute comes in the later chapter on the divine nature.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘those derivations rest on contested assumptions’, agree that they need defending — Feser says so himself — but point out that the objection has now changed. It is no longer ‘a first-cause argument *can’t* tell you anything about the cause’; it’s ‘I dispute step 16 (or 28, or 42)’. That is a specific premise you can examine together. Also note that an impersonal force or quantum field has potentials (it can be in different states), so it can’t be what is purely actual.

objections.title: The universe may not have had a beginning
objections.whoRaises: Readers who assume every theistic argument is a ‘Big Bang’ argument; defenders of eternal or cyclic cosmologies
objections.objection: The argument says that if you trace causes back in time you reach God at the beginning of the universe. But we don’t know the universe had a beginning — the Big Bang might have come from an earlier universe, and an infinite multiverse might have no start at all.
objections.reply: This is a misreading. Feser explicitly **grants**, for argument’s sake, that the universe — or a series of universes — might stretch infinitely into the past. Aristotle himself believed the world was eternal. Whether the cosmos had a beginning is **irrelevant** because the argument concerns a **hierarchical** series of causes that sustain things **here and now**, not a linear series running back through time. Even in a beginningless universe, the water in your coffee exists at this moment only because its potential to exist as water is being actualized at this moment.
objections.pushback: If they still insist ‘but the chain has to go back to God at some point’, draw two diagrams: a horizontal line of events (linear — can be infinite) and a vertical stack of dependencies at a single moment (hierarchical — needs a top). Ask them which one the argument uses. Beginningless-multiverse cosmologies speak only to the horizontal line.

objections.title: Fallacy of composition: the whole universe needn’t have a cause
objections.whoRaises: Bertrand Russell–style critics; introductory philosophy textbooks
objections.objection: Even if every part of the universe has a cause, it doesn’t follow that the universe as a whole has one. Inferring a cause of the whole from causes of the parts is a fallacy of composition.
objections.reply: No premise of the argument is about the universe as a whole. It begins with **any single object existing now** — a stone, a cup of coffee — and shows that for *that one thing* to exist even for a moment, a purely actual cause must be actualizing it at that moment. Feser does go on to say this applies to every material thing, and so to the universe as a whole — but that is a **consequence** drawn from the argument, not a premise it relies on.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘generalizing from the coffee to everything is still composition’, point out that it’s not composition but ordinary universal instantiation: the reasoning applies to *each* thing with a potential for existence, one at a time, because each has that potential. No claim about the whole is inferred from the parts.

objections.title: ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’
objections.whoRaises: Popular atheist writers; the most common objection in casual conversation
objections.objection: The argument says everything needs a cause, then exempts God. If God can exist uncaused, why not the universe? This is special pleading.
objections.reply:
Two points.

1. The argument never says ‘everything has a cause’. Its principle is that **whatever goes from potential to actual** needs an actualizer.
2. The exemption is not arbitrary; it follows from the principle’s own rationale. Things need causes *because* they have potentials that must be actualized. What is **purely actual** has no potentials — nothing in it that needs to be, or even could be, actualized. So it is the one thing that neither needs nor could have a cause.

The universe, by contrast, is full of potentiality — it changes constantly — so it is exactly the sort of thing that needs an actualizer.
objections.pushback: If they reply ‘there’s no real difference between those two principles’, give Feser’s analogy: that’s like saying there’s no real difference between ‘all triangles have three sides’ and ‘all geometrical figures have three sides’. The first is restricted to a kind, for a reason; the second isn’t.

objections.title: ‘The potential-to-actual formulation is an ad hoc dodge’
objections.whoRaises: Critics trying to rescue the ‘What caused God?’ objection
objections.objection: Theists only avoid saying ‘everything has a cause’ because they know it invites ‘What caused God?’. The careful formulation was invented to escape the objection.
objections.reply:
Feser identifies three problems.

1. **Ad hominem.** Even if the motive were suspect, that wouldn’t show the principle is false or the argument unsound. Motives don’t refute arguments.
2. **Historically false.** For over twenty-three centuries — Aristotle, Aquinas, and their successors to today — defenders of the argument have *always* stated it this way. It wasn’t cooked up to answer modern critics.
3. **Not ad hoc at all.** The principle falls straight out of Aristotle’s analysis of change, independent of any argument for God. You don’t need to believe in God to find it implausible that a mere potential could actualize itself.

If anything is ad hoc, it is the attempt to save an objection aimed at a straw man.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘fine, but it still conveniently lets God off the hook’, ask them to state a principle that would require a purely actual being to have a cause. They will have to show that pure actuality has some potential needing actualization — which contradicts what ‘purely actual’ means.

objections.title: Hume: we can conceive of something popping into existence uncaused
objections.whoRaises: David Hume and empiricists following him
objections.objection: I can imagine an empty space in which a stone suddenly appears with nothing causing it. Whatever is conceivable is possible, so an uncaused beginning is possible — and then perhaps something can go from potential to actual with no actualizer.
objections.reply:
Feser gives three replies.

1. **Imagining without a cause isn’t imagining no cause.** Picturing the stone appearing is only conceiving of it *without also conceiving of* its cause. You can think of a trilateral without thinking of it as a triangle, or of a man without thinking of his height — but no trilateral fails to be a triangle and no man lacks a height. Conceiving A without B is not conceiving A existing without B.
2. **Anscombe’s point.** What makes the scenario one of *coming into existence* rather than the stone’s being *transported* from somewhere? The only difference lies in the kind of cause involved (being made versus being moved). So spelling out the scenario brings causation back in.
3. **Experience strongly supports the principle.** We find causes when we look; when we don’t (an unsolved murder) we reasonably assume they are there. If the principle were false, nothing would be needed to produce anything — as W. Norris Clarke says, elephants and hotels could appear on your lawn, and should do so constantly. They don’t. The best explanation is that potentiality by its nature requires actualization.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘maybe the regularity is just a brute fact’, point out that it would then be a colossal, unexplained coincidence that the world behaves exactly as it would if the principle were true. An empiricist of all people should follow the evidence, and the evidence overwhelmingly favors the principle.

objections.title: Kant: causality applies only within experience
objections.whoRaises: Immanuel Kant and Kantian critics
objections.objection: We learn about causation from the empirical world. Even if the principle holds there, what entitles us to extend it beyond all possible experience to something immaterial, timeless and unobservable?
objections.reply: We do learn the principle from experience, but that doesn’t limit its scope. We conclude that the things we experience need causes not **because we experience them** but **because they are merely potential until made actual**. The principle that no potential actualizes itself is fully general, so it applies wherever there is potentiality, observable or not. Feser’s analogy: we learn Euclidean geometry from diagrams, usually in black ink, but its theorems apply to figures of any color or none. Restricting causality to what we can experience is like restricting geometry to figures we can see.
objections.pushback: If they press the full Kantian view that causality is just a category our minds impose, note that the argument can start from change in our own experience — which even a Kantian grants — and that the Kantian theory itself makes sweeping claims about how minds and appearances are related (causal-sounding claims) that go beyond experience. More in the later chapter on objections.

objections.title: Russell: physics has no place for causes
objections.whoRaises: Bertrand Russell (‘On the Notion of Cause’, 1912) and eliminativists about causation
objections.objection: Mature physics describes the world with differential equations relating events. Nowhere in the equations is there a ‘cause’ — just a formula. Causation is a pre-scientific relic.
objections.reply:
Feser gives four replies.

1. **It proves too much.** ‘Event’, ‘law’ and ‘explanation’ don’t appear in the equations either, yet science can’t do without them. As Jonathan Schaffer puts it, this is like saying mathematics has eliminated the variable because the word ‘variable’ is never written in the equations.
2. **Physics does use causal notions.** C. B. Martin notes that fundamental particles have dispositions — tendencies to produce effects when they interact in certain ways.
3. **Other sciences clearly use causation**, and they aren’t reducible to physics — biology, the social sciences, arguably chemistry. And naturalists themselves defend causal theories of knowledge, perception and meaning.
4. **Physics isn’t exhaustive.** It captures only the mathematically describable structure of things; the later Russell admitted it says nothing about the intrinsic nature of what changes. Inferring that nothing lies beyond its reach is like concluding there’s no wood because your metal detector didn’t beep.

Moreover, something must make the world actually follow these equations, and if what the equations describe is real change, that change is actualization of potential — causation.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘fine, causation is only in our experience, not in reality’, reply that then causation is at least in our experience — one experience actualizing the next, as when setting up an experiment is followed by observing the result — and that is enough actualization of potential to start the argument. And our knowledge of physics depends on the world causally affecting our senses.

objections.title: Newton’s law of inertia: motion continues without a cause
objections.whoRaises: Critics of Aristotle’s ‘whatever is moved is moved by another’; many philosophers of physics
objections.objection: Newton’s first law says a body in uniform motion keeps moving with no force acting on it. So change (continued motion) happens without any cause, and the principle of causality is false.
objections.reply:
Three responses.

1. **Different question.** Inertia concerns events in time — how molecules move through a cup. The argument is about what actualizes a thing’s **existence** at a moment — what makes these components constitute a water molecule right now. Newton’s law presupposes such things; it can’t explain their existence.
2. **Laws presuppose natures.** A law of nature is shorthand for how things with a certain nature tend to behave. What makes it the case that there are things with *this* nature, following *this* law rather than another? What actualizes that? Mechanics can’t say.
3. **Mathematical abstraction.** As James Weisheipl argues, mathematical physics doesn’t prove inertia; it *assumes* it. To write equations, it treats uniform motion as a baseline needing no explanation and quantifies only *changes* in motion. Newton set aside physical causes and sought quantities that could be equated. So such physics can neither affirm nor deny causal realities.

Inertia therefore doesn’t refute the principle of causality — it *couldn’t*. However inertia is interpreted, it must be made compatible with the principle, which reaches deeper than physics.
objections.pushback: If they ask what the Aristotelian does say about inertial motion, mention Feser’s footnote: following Aquinas’ idea of motions that follow ‘spontaneously’ from a thing’s nature, some contemporary Aristotelians treat inertia as the way a body tends to move given its form. The efficient cause is what generated the body with that nature — and ultimately what sustains it in being. So inertial motion isn’t uncaused; it just doesn’t need a continuously pushing external mover.

objections.title: Einstein’s block universe: change is an illusion
objections.whoRaises: Eternalist interpreters of relativity (following Minkowski); some physicists and philosophers of time
objections.objection: On the four-dimensional block universe, past, present and future are all equally real, like places on a map. Nothing ever passes from potential to actual; the flow of time is just how consciousness represents things. So the argument’s first premise fails.
objections.reply:
Feser notes that the block interpretation is controversial even among physicists (he points to Lee Smolin), but he doesn’t need to settle it.

1. **Self-undermining.** Relativity rests on observation and experiment — making predictions and then testing them, going from ignorance to knowledge. All that is change. So denying change entirely undercuts the evidence for the theory itself (a point made by Richard Healey). At most one could say change exists only in the mind, and change in the mind is still actualization of potential.
2. **Existence still needs an actualizer.** Even if nothing changed anywhere, a thing’s very existence involves actualized potential. The block universe as a whole — this block rather than some other, or none — would still need an actualizer distinct from it.

Relativity at most affects **how** we apply the principle of causality, not **whether** we must.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘change in the mind is also an illusion’, point out that an illusion is itself a mental event that comes and goes, and that coming to believe the block theory is a change of mind. Denying all change is not a position anyone can coherently hold — any more than Parmenides could.

objections.title: Quantum indeterminism means some events have no cause
objections.whoRaises: Popular science writers; some physicists
objections.objection: Quantum events are fundamentally probabilistic. Nothing determines when a particular atom decays or where an electron is detected. So there are changes without causes.
objections.reply:
Some point out that de Broglie–Bohm’s hidden-variable interpretation makes quantum mechanics deterministic after all. But the deeper point is that **causation doesn’t require determinism**. A cause must make its effect *intelligible*, not *necessary*. Even on the indeterministic Copenhagen interpretation, as Robert Koons notes, every transition has causal antecedents — the prior wave state, or the prior state plus the measurement.

And more fundamentally: mathematical physics abstracts from causal and qualitative content. That a theory assigns no deterministic cause doesn’t show there is no cause; **absence from the representation isn’t a representation of absence**.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘but a cause that could have failed to produce the effect isn’t really a cause’, use Phil Dowe’s example: if I bring a bucket of lead-210 into your room and you get radiation sickness, I’m responsible — and I can’t be morally responsible for what I didn’t cause. Denying indeterministic causation would let me off the hook, which is absurd.

objections.title: The Bell inequalities show uncaused correlations
objections.whoRaises: Philosophers of physics; popularizers of quantum entanglement
objections.objection: Experiments confirming violations of the Bell inequalities show correlations between distant measurements that can’t be explained by any common cause or by signals traveling at or below light speed. So there are correlations with no causal explanation.
objections.reply:
Feser notes several proposals that preserve causality: allowing causal influences faster than light, backward causation, an absolute reference frame, or a law according to which the correlations hold (options discussed by Koons and Alexander Pruss). All raise questions, as does every interpretation of quantum mechanics.

But the decisive point is methodological. Quantum theory is a mathematical representation that by its nature leaves causal content out. That it doesn’t *show* a cause is no evidence there isn’t one — just as a black-and-white drawing is no evidence that the scene lacks color. And the entangled systems themselves exist and have their natures only because their potentials are being actualized.
objections.pushback: If they say you’re just ‘hiding behind metaphysics’, note that the burden runs the other way: the objection claims physics proves something (no cause) that physics’ method is incapable of detecting either way. Feser’s point is that such objections aren’t even well-formulated.

objections.title: Virtual particles pop into existence from nothing
objections.whoRaises: Popular cosmology (e.g. claims that a ‘universe from nothing’ is possible)
objections.objection: Quantum field theory says particles come into and go out of existence at random in the vacuum. That is something coming into being with no cause.
objections.reply: Pruss suggests either a hidden-variable account or treating the system described by quantum field theory as the indeterministic cause of these events. More importantly, a quantum vacuum isn’t *nothing*: it is a physical system with a definite structure, governed by laws, and bursting with potentialities. Particles emerging from it are **potentials of the field being actualized** — exactly what the principle of causality addresses, not a counterexample to it. And the field itself exists here and now with that nature only because its potential for existence is being actualized.
objections.pushback: If they insist the events are random, return to the point that randomness isn’t causelessness (indeterministic causation) and that laws describe the behavior of things with natures — so the question becomes: what actualizes the existence of a field with *this* nature?

objections.title: Radioactive decay is uncaused
objections.whoRaises: Philosophers of science; popular critics
objections.objection: A lead-210 atom may decay into mercury-206 with no outside interference, at a time nothing determines. Only a probability can be assigned. So the decay has no cause.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘calling it the atom’s nature is just a label’, reply that it is exactly what physicists appeal to: lead-210 has this half-life *because* it is lead-210 and not some other isotope. That is grounding in the kind of thing it is — which is what a formal cause is.

objections.title: Aristotelianism was refuted by modern science
objections.whoRaises: Popular histories of the Scientific Revolution; many scientists
objections.objection: Modern science overthrew Aristotle. An Aristotelian argument for God is as obsolete as Aristotelian astronomy.
objections.reply: Feser calls this sloppy: it lumps together very different ideas. ‘Aristotelianism’ labels a huge body of scientific, philosophical, theological and political claims. Some specifically **scientific** ones — geocentrism, the four elements, natural places — really were refuted. But the claim that change is actualization of potential is **metaphysical**, and science hasn’t refuted it. On the contrary, science presupposes change (observation and experiment involve moving from one experience to another), so every possible scientific theory presupposes the actualization of potential. The book’s arguments rest on these deeper metaphysical foundations, not on revisable scientific claims.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘metaphysics has been replaced by science’, ask what scientific experiment could establish that only science yields knowledge. That claim is itself philosophical — and a later chapter shows science rests on metaphysical foundations it cannot justify on its own.

objections.title: Eddington’s two tables: the examples are scientifically naïve
objections.whoRaises: Readers of Arthur Eddington’s The Nature of the Physical World; scientistic critics
objections.objection: Physics shows a desk is really a cloud of particles in mostly empty space; cups ‘rest’ on it only because particles keep colliding. So talk of a desk holding up a cup, a floor holding up a desk, etc., gets the science wrong, and an argument built on such examples is poorly grounded.
objections.reply:
Feser thinks this sounds sophisticated but is silly, for three reasons.

1. **No competition.** It assumes common sense and physics compete. That the floor, desk and cup are made of colliding particles doesn’t mean the floor doesn’t really hold up the desk; physics just describes the **mechanism** by which it does.
2. **Selective.** No one accuses an engineer (how thick a foundation must be to support a building) or a doctor (how a herniated disk fails to support the spine) of outdated science for ignoring particle physics.
3. **Irrelevant.** The examples were only meant to introduce actualization of potential and the linear/hierarchical distinction. Those concepts apply whether we speak of desks or particle clouds. The details affect **how**, not **whether**, we apply them. We don’t object to a physicist’s thought experiment about riding a light beam that photons are too small to sit on.
objections.pushback: If they still worry, restate the example at the particle level: the cup’s particles are held at a certain height by electromagnetic interactions with the desk’s particles, which depend on the floor’s, and so on — still a hierarchical series of actualizers, just described more finely. And the deeper series (of existence) runs from molecules to atoms to subatomic particles anyway.

objections.title: There are no truly simultaneous causes
objections.whoRaises: Humean critics; physics-minded skeptics
objections.objection: Hierarchical series rely on causes acting simultaneously with their effects. But precise measurement would show a time lag between stick and stone, desk and cup. And if immediate causes were simultaneous, every causal chain would collapse into one instant. Besides, relativity makes simultaneity observer-relative.
objections.reply:
Feser answers point by point.

1. **Simultaneous isn’t instantaneous.** Pushing a stone takes time, but the stick’s moving it and its being moved are one event. Clarke: it takes time to push a chair across a room, but there is no time between the pushing and the chair’s being pushed.
2. **Immediate causes are simultaneous with effects.** Following Mumford and Anjum: it isn’t ball A’s earlier motion that strictly causes B’s, but A’s impact on B, which is one event with B’s being impacted. It isn’t the throw that immediately breaks the glass but the brick pressing into it.
3. **No collapse.** Distinguish causation *within* one process from one process setting up conditions for another. Sugar dissolving in tea, the tea being drunk, the tea being digested: each is a causal process, but the dissolving doesn’t cause the drinking in the same sense; it just sets the stage.
4. **Relativity is irrelevant.** Relativity of simultaneity concerns distinct, spatially separated events; here cause and effect are parts of the same event at the same place.
5. **Not the point anyway.** What makes a series hierarchical is derivative, instrumental power, not simultaneity. And the argument’s key series concerns a thing’s existence at an instant — which raises no issue of duration at all.
objections.pushback: If they keep pressing on timing, grant it and move to point 5: ‘Forget stones and sticks. At this instant, the water exists as water rather than as separate hydrogen and oxygen. What actualizes that?’ The question arises at any instant, however events are timed.

objections.title: Infinite series are possible, so why not an infinite hierarchical regress?
objections.whoRaises: Graham Oppy (Arguing about Gods) and others who say no reason is given to rule out infinite regress
objections.objection: Mathematics is full of infinite series — the natural numbers go on forever without a first. Aquinas and Feser give no real reason why a causal series couldn’t do the same.
objections.reply: Oppy ignores the crucial role of **instrumental** causation. Mathematical series involve no instrumental and primary causes — indeed no causation at all — so they’re not relevant counterexamples. Aristotelians don’t reject infinite series as such: they allow infinite mathematical series and even beginningless *linear* causal series. What they deny is a hierarchical series with no source of underived power. In such a series every member acts only by power received; if nothing has the power unreceived, nothing acts at all. An infinitely long brush handle still can’t move itself; an infinite hall of mirrors still needs a real face. Without a first cause we just pass the explanatory buck forever.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘each member is explained by the previous one, so every member is explained’, reply that in a per se series, no member explains the *power* it passes along — it only transmits what it receives. Explaining each transmission by another transmission never explains where the power comes from, just as adding more boxcars never explains how the train moves.

objections.title: Calling causes ‘instrumental’ begs the question
objections.whoRaises: Jordan Howard Sobel (Logic and Theism)
objections.objection: To call the intermediate causes ‘instruments’ already assumes there is some first cause using them. We have no reason to think things depend on hierarchical series of that kind unless we already accept theism.
objections.reply: No question is begged. Calling something an instrumental cause means only that it **derives its causal power from something else**. That description doesn’t itself say that a series of such causes can’t go to infinity, or that some cause has underived power — those are conclusions argued for separately. Even a skeptic understands that a stick can’t move a stone under its own power, whatever he goes on to say about whether a regress of moved movers must end.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘but why believe ordinary things depend on hierarchical series at all?’, go back to the water: its matter could be separate gases, so its being water now is an actualized potential; bonding and atomic structure just push the question down a level. That dependence is shown by analyzing ordinary cases, not by presupposing God.

objections.title: Unmoved isn’t unmovable: the first mover might have unrealized potentials
objections.whoRaises: Sophisticated critics of the attribute derivations
objections.objection: Grant a first actualizer that isn’t being actualized while it acts. Why must it be *purely* actual? It could have potentials that are actualized at other times, or never. Then it wouldn’t be one, eternal, immaterial or perfect.
objections.reply:
The regress that matters is of actualizers of **existence**. The first actualizer is first because it actualizes others’ existence without its own existence needing to be actualized. Suppose it had a potential that must be actualized for it to exist. What actualizes it?

- **Something else?** Then it isn’t the first actualizer after all.
- **A purely actual part of itself?** Then *that part* is the real first actualizer, and the potential ‘part’ is just its first effect.
- **A part mixing act and potency?** Then what actualizes *that part’s* potentials? Another mixed part — a vicious regress.

So there is no coherent first actualizer of existence that isn’t purely actual. To admit a first actualizer at all is to admit pure actuality, with all the attributes that follow from it.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘maybe its extra potentials have nothing to do with its existence — they’re just unused capacities’, reply that any unrealized potential makes a thing a composite of act and potency, and a composite exists only if something makes that combination actual. For the supposed first actualizer, that ‘something’ must be either another being or a part of itself — which lands you straight back in the three-way dilemma. (The Neo-Platonic and Thomistic chapters, and the chapter on the divine attributes, develop this further.)

objections.title: A purely actual actualizer is incoherent — to cause is to change
objections.whoRaises: Critics who argue causation always involves the cause’s own change
objections.objection: Anything that actualizes another thing must itself undergo change in doing so, so it must have potentials being actualized. A cause that acts without changing is a contradiction.
objections.reply:
Three responses.

1. **It begs the question.** The argument claims to prove no potential could be actualized without a purely actual actualizer. If the premises are true and the logic valid, the conclusion is true and so coherent. The critic must find a false premise or bad inference, not just assert the conclusion is impossible. Otherwise the argument shows a purely actual actualizer is possible, since actual.
2. **Fallacy of accident.** Observed causes change when they act — your arm moves to move the stick. But that’s a contingent feature of the causes we meet, not an essential feature of causing. Compare: every U.S. president so far has been under seven feet tall, but it doesn’t follow no one taller *could* be president.
3. **No contradiction.** An ‘immortal mortal’ is contradictory; a ‘purely actual actualizer’ is simply something that actualizes without being actualized. And we can say *why* our causes must change: they are **limited** — an arm is actually here and only potentially there, so to get the stick there its own potential must be actualized. Pure act has no such limits.
objections.pushback: If they ask ‘but how can something act without changing?’, compare it to the way a truth ‘makes’ a conclusion follow without anything happening to it, or the way an attractive object draws you without itself moving (Aristotle’s own image). These are imperfect analogies, but they show that ‘acting’ and ‘undergoing change’ are not the same concept.

objections.title: Why not let the universe, energy, or the laws of physics be the purely actual thing?
objections.whoRaises: Modern naturalists (a common response, not discussed by name in the chapter)
objections.objection: Fine — something has to be at the bottom of the hierarchy. Why not the universe itself, or conserved mass-energy, or the fundamental laws of physics? Why go beyond nature?
objections.reply: Apply the chapter’s own test: does the candidate have any **potentiality**? The universe changes constantly, so it is shot through with potentiality. Mass-energy takes different forms at different times — it is potentially otherwise than it is. Fundamental particles and fields have states they could be in but aren’t. And laws, the chapter argues, are shorthand for how things with certain natures behave; they don’t exist on their own, and the question remains what makes it the case that things with *these* natures exist rather than others. Anything with potential needs an actualizer, so none of these can be the terminus. And whatever is purely actual must be immutable, eternal and immaterial — unlike anything physical.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘maybe the universe’s existence is just a brute fact’, point out that the argument doesn’t need the principle of sufficient reason; it needs only the principle that a mere potential can’t actualize itself. A brute-fact universe would be a vast collection of potentials actualized by nothing — the very thing Hume’s ‘pop into existence’ scenario tried and failed to make coherent.

objections.title: ‘God of the gaps’: science will eventually explain it
objections.whoRaises: Scientifically minded skeptics (a common modern objection)
objections.objection: Every time religion has pointed to something science couldn’t explain, science eventually explained it. The ‘sustaining cause’ is just another gap that physics will fill.
objections.reply: The argument doesn’t point to a gap in scientific knowledge; it points to something every scientific explanation **presupposes**. Science explains how things behave given that they exist with certain natures and follow certain laws. The Aristotelian question is what actualizes the existence of things with those natures here and now. Filling in more physics (a deeper particle, a new field) just adds more members to the hierarchical series — each with potentials needing actualization. No amount of physics can reach the terminus, because anything physical is a mix of act and potency. That is why Feser treats objections from physics as not even well-formulated: physics’ method abstracts from exactly what the argument is about.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘then the argument is unfalsifiable’, reply that it can be challenged the normal philosophical way — by attacking a premise or an inference, and many have tried. Being beyond the reach of experiments is not a defect; so are the laws of logic and the claim that only experiments yield knowledge.
